---

A runtime that turns a plain **JSON config into live cascivo UI**. `CascivoView` takes a `ViewConfig` object and renders the real components — so AI agents (and no-code tooling) can emit data instead of writing TSX.

## Usage

A `ViewConfig` is named regions of component nodes; each node names a component (`component`), plus optional `props`, `children`, data bindings, and event wiring:

```tsx
import { CascivoView, type ViewConfig } from '@cascivo/render'

const view: ViewConfig = {
  view: {
    regions: {
      main: [
        {
          component: 'Card',
          children: [
            {
              component: 'Badge',
              props: { variant: 'secondary' },
              bind: { children: '$data.count' },
            },
            {
              component: 'Button',
              props: { variant: 'primary' },
              children: 'Invite',
              events: { onClick: '$actions.invite' },
            },
          ],
        },
      ],
    },
  },
}

export function App() {
  return (
    <CascivoView
      config={view}
      data={{ count: 42 }}
      actions={{ invite: () => console.log('invite') }}
    />
  )
}
```

The JSON stays fully serializable: live values come from the host via `bind` (`"$data.users.active"` resolves a dot-path into the `data` prop) and handlers via `events` (`"$actions.invite"` looks up the `actions` prop) — never from the config itself. Strings can be i18n refs (`{ "$t": "catalog.key" }`), resolved through `@cascivo/i18n`. `config` also accepts a `Signal<ViewConfig>`, so a view can be swapped live.

Nodes resolve against a built-in component map of 74 cascivo components (Button, Card, Badge, Input, Select, Modal, Tabs, DataTable, Form, …) — see `component-map.ts` for the full list.

### Your own components, and charts

Pass `components` to render names beyond the built-in set: charts, or your app's own components. They are looked up before the built-ins, the validator accepts them, and their props are passed through unchecked:

```tsx
import { Kpi, LineChart } from '@cascivo/charts'

;<CascivoView config={view} data={data} components={{ Kpi, LineChart }} />
```

`@cascivo/render` does not depend on `@cascivo/charts`, so only an app that renders charts installs it. Validate such a view with the same names: `validateView(view, { components: ['Kpi', 'LineChart'] })`, and read it as Markdown with `viewToMarkdown(view, { components: { Kpi, LineChart } })`.

## Validation

Every render validates first. Invalid configs **throw** by default with exact paths; pass `onInvalid="render"` to show errors inline instead (playground mode). `validateView` is exported for validating before rendering:

```ts
import { validateView } from '@cascivo/render'

const { valid, errors } = validateView(view) // errors: { path, message }[]
```

Unknown components (with a did-you-mean hint), malformed nodes, and prop values that don't match the generated per-component prop schemas are reported with exact paths, so generated views fail loudly rather than rendering garbage.

On a server, import it from `@cascivo/render/validate`. That entry has no React and no components, only the validator and the prop schemas it checks against, so it runs in a Cloudflare Worker, an edge function or a Node script:

```ts
import { validateView } from '@cascivo/render/validate'

// In an AI tool: hand the errors back to the model, which fixes them and calls again.
const { valid, errors } = validateView(modelOutput)
```

`cascivo create --framework cloudflare --example agent` builds an assistant around exactly this: the Worker validates each view the model produces, and the page renders it with `<CascivoView>`.

Pair it with the MCP server's bound-vocabulary grammar (`get_view_grammar`) and `scaffold_view` for the full anti-hallucination loop: the model can only emit components and props that exist, and `validateView` is the enforcement backstop. `cascivo generate <config.json>` converts a validated `ViewConfig` into owned TSX when you want to graduate from JSON to source.

## Component catalog

The renderable vocabulary is also published as data, generated from the same manifests the validator uses, so other tools can target cascivo without importing React:

```ts
import catalog from '@cascivo/render/schema/catalog.v1.json' with { type: 'json' }
import a2ui from '@cascivo/render/schema/a2ui/v0_9/catalog.json' with { type: 'json' }
```

- `schema/catalog.v1.json` is the protocol-neutral catalog: one entry per renderable component.
- `schema/a2ui/v0_9/catalog.json` is the same catalog as an [A2UI](https://a2ui.org) v0.9 custom catalog. Its `catalogId` is `https://cascivo.com/a2ui/v0_9/catalog.json`, and the file is served there.

Every prop of a component is sorted into one of four kinds:

| Kind      | Meaning                                                                                                                                              |
| --------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `props`   | Data props, each with a JSON Schema                                                                                                                  |
| `slots`   | Child content, with arity `one` or `many` (`text: true` when it also takes a string, as `children` does; `implicit: true` when inferred from source) |
| `events`  | Callbacks an agent can wire to an action                                                                                                             |
| `omitted` | Props that cannot cross the wire (functions, DOM refs), with the reason                                                                              |

`validateView` also checks the shape of object and array props, such as `DataTable` `columns`: nested fields by presence and type, so an unknown nested field is allowed.

Regenerate both files with `pnpm regen` (or `pnpm schema:generate && vp check --fix`); CI fails when the committed files drift from the manifests. `pnpm schema:check` runs the generator unit tests.

## Render A2UI

`@cascivo/render/a2ui/v0_9` renders [A2UI](https://a2ui.org) v0.9 messages with cascivo components. It is our own renderer, not `@a2ui/react`: that package brings lit, zod, a second signals store and custom elements. The store holds messages as signals, so a data change re-renders only the nodes bound to it.

```tsx
import {
  A2uiSurface,
  createA2uiStore,
  defaultCatalogs,
  defaultCatalogSpecs,
} from '@cascivo/render/a2ui/v0_9'

const store = createA2uiStore({ catalogs: defaultCatalogSpecs })

// Feed it each message the agent sends, already parsed from JSON. `apply` never throws and
// returns the errors to send back to the agent.
export const feed = (raw: unknown) => store.apply(raw)

export function Agent({ send }: { send: (action: unknown) => void }) {
  return <A2uiSurface store={store} surfaceId="main" catalogs={defaultCatalogs} onAction={send} />
}
```

The entry has no `'use client'`; in React Server Components apps import `A2uiSurface` from a client module.

### Catalogs

- The **cascivo catalog** (`cascivoCatalog`, spec `cascivoCatalogSpec`, id `A2UI_CATALOG_ID`) lets an agent target real cascivo components, the same vocabulary `validateView` checks.
- The **basic catalog** (`basicCatalog`, spec `basicCatalogSpec`, id `BASIC_CATALOG_ID`) is A2UI's standard set, drawn with cascivo components.

A surface uses the catalog its `createSurface` message names; the store only knows the catalogs passed to `createA2uiStore`, so inline catalogs are refused.

### Security and limits

- Every message is validated against the catalog spec before it reaches state; a bad one becomes an `A2uiErrorMessage`, never an exception.
- URLs that reach `href`, `src` or `window.open` are checked, and unsafe ones are dropped.
- A value bound in from the data model, or computed by a function, is checked against the prop's schema when it renders; one that does not fit is dropped and reported as `RENDER_ERROR`. `{$t}` translation refs are refused: an agent cannot know the host's i18n keys.
- `openUrl` runs only as an action's `functionCall`, from a user's click (where the browser has `navigator.userActivation`, only while it is active, so an action the agent triggers by closing a Modal cannot open a page); anywhere else the spec refuses it.
- Each component renders inside an error boundary: one that throws (an adapter of your own too) renders nothing and reports `RENDER_ERROR` once, and the rest of the surface and the host keep rendering. The next data-model write retries it. A cascivo component whose required prop has no data yet renders a Skeleton until it arrives.
- An action's `a2uiClientDataModel` carries only the acting surface's data model, never another agent's.
- `createA2uiStore({ limits })` overrides `DEFAULT_A2UI_LIMITS`: surfaces, components, id length, data nodes, render depth and `maxRenderNodes` (default 20000, so shared ids cannot fan a tree out exponentially).
- The `regex` function refuses patterns with more than 2 quantifiers (an exact `{n}` does not count), repeat counts above 99, backreferences, nested quantifiers, and values over 256 characters.

### Custom adapters

An `A2uiAdapter` receives an `AdapterInput` (`component`, `prop`, `slot`, `children`, `resolve`, `typeOf`, `componentOf`, `writer`, `action`, `failingChecks`, `report`). Call `slot()` and `children()` at most once each, synchronously while the adapter runs, and place each returned node once. Later calls render nothing, because the render-node budget counts every node.

## Install

```sh
pnpm add @cascivo/render
```
